summary: Describes a way to automatically, authenticatedly update DNSSEC trust anchors, protecting against compromise of N-1 of N keys. It needs resolver management changes and one new flag bit in the DNSKEY record. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A DNSSEC resolver needs trusted keys to check signed DNS data, and replacing those keys manually can be difficult. This RFC defines how a resolver can accept a new key after a waiting period and stop trusting a key that revokes itself.

questions: how do resolvers update trust anchors
how do dnssec trust anchors update automatically
what is the dnskey revoke bit
subtitle: How a validating resolver can accept and retire DNSSEC trust-anchor keys automatically.

tldr.problem: A DNSSEC resolver needs trust anchors to validate signed branches of the DNS tree. Replacing many trust-anchor keys by hand is difficult, and a compromised key must be removable without letting it discard other keys.
tldr.mechanism: An existing anchor can validate a DNSKEY RRSet containing a new SEP key, which is accepted only after a hold-down period. A REVOKE bit lets a key revoke itself through a signed DNSKEY RRSet.
tldr.outcome: Resolvers can update keys without changing how they resolve names, but initial configuration remains outside the RFC. Recovery requires at least one uncompromised valid anchor; RFC 5011 is an Internet Standard.

sections.title: The Trust-Anchor Management Problem
sections.content:
The Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) can secure branches of the Domain Name System (DNS) tree that begin at different trust points. A trust anchor associates a trust-point name with a public key that a resolver accepts as a starting point for validation.

A resolver may need many trust anchors, and operators must also replace keys when they roll them over. RFC 5011 describes automatic updates to keys at an already configured trust point. It does not describe initial trust-anchor configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: A resolver needs a trusted key before it can check DNSSEC data at a trust point. This RFC automates later key changes, but not the first setup of that trust point.

sections.title: Revocation and the Add Hold-Down
sections.content:
An existing trust anchor can authenticate a new Secure Entry Point (SEP) key when the key appears in a validated DNSKEY resource-record set (RRSet). The resolver starts a timer and records which existing keys validated the set. It does not accept the new key until the hold-down expires and it has fetched and validated a later DNSKEY RRSet that still contains the key.

A key is revoked when the resolver sees that key in a self-signed DNSKEY RRSet with its REVOKE bit set. Revocation is immediate and permanent; the key may then be used only to validate the signature that proves its own revocation.

The hold-down reduces the risk that one compromised key adds a malicious key and revokes good keys. It cannot stop an attacker who controls a compromised key from intercepting data and hiding the real DNSKEY RRSet from a resolver.
sections.plainLanguage: A resolver waits before accepting a newly advertised key and checks that the key remains present in validated data. A key can revoke itself, after which the resolver no longer accepts it as a trust anchor.

sections.title: Refresh Timing and the REVOKE Flag
sections.content:
A resolver configured for automatic updates must query the trust point's DNSKEY RRSet and related signatures on a schedule. The query interval is no more often than once per hour and no less often than the minimum of 15 days, half the original TTL, and half the RRSIG expiration interval, subject to the formula in the RFC.

The add hold-down is 30 days or the expiration time of the original TTL for the first RRSet containing the new key, whichever is greater. The remove hold-down is 30 days. A compliant resolver must be able to manage at least five SEP keys for each trust point.

The wire-format change is the REVOKE flag in bit 8 of the DNSKEY Flags field. A set bit, together with an RRSIG made by that key over the DNSKEY RRSet, makes the key permanently invalid for other purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: The resolver checks for key changes on a schedule and waits at least the specified hold-down before accepting a new key. The REVOKE flag marks a key that must no longer be trusted.

sections.title: The Resolver's Key States
sections.content:
The RFC defines six states for a key at a trust point: Start, AddPend, Valid, Missing, Revoked, and Removed. A new SEP key moves from Start to AddPend when it appears in validated data, then to Valid after it remains present through the add hold-down.

If a validated RRSet omits a valid key, the key enters Missing; it remains a valid trust-point key, but the RFC calls this state abnormal. A signed REVOKE flag moves a key to Revoked. After the remove hold-down, its stored information may be purged and it enters Removed, which is not a valid trust-anchor state.
sections.plainLanguage: The resolver tracks a key from first sight, through a waiting period, to valid use. It can also track a missing key, a revoked key, and a key whose old state has been removed.

sections.title: Adding, Replacing, and Deleting Keys
sections.content:
The suggested arrangement has an active key that signs the DNSKEY RRSet and a standby key that is available for a later rollover. To add a key, the operator publishes its DNSKEY record and signs the RRSet with the existing anchor; resolvers add the new key after their hold-down process.

To retire a key, the operator sets its REVOKE bit and signs the RRSet with that key and any other active anchor. The revoked key should remain in the RRSet for at least the remove hold-down. During a rollover, a new standby key can be added while the active key is revoked.

If every anchor at a trust point is revoked, the resolver treats that trust point as deleted. The RFC also permits a resolver, as a local decision, to delete a subordinate trust point after 180 days when it validly chains to a superior configured trust point.
sections.plainLanguage: An operator can add a standby key before retiring an active key. If every key at a trust point is revoked, the resolver stops treating that point as configured.

sections.title: What Compromised Keys Can and Cannot Do
sections.content:
The zone owner publishes keys, but the resolver owner decides whether to accept automatic updates. Resolver owners may disable updates for particular trust points, in which case they need another way to update the keys.

The scheme allows recovery while at least one valid trust-anchor key remains uncompromised. If every trust-anchor key at a point is compromised, all resolvers need a manual or other out-of-band update. The RFC recognizes that accepting updates from DNS data may be less secure than a manual process, but argues that it is no worse than the existing management problem.
sections.plainLanguage: The resolver owner controls whether automatic updates are accepted. Automatic recovery is possible while at least one valid key remains uncompromised; if all are compromised, an outside update is needed.
